Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

This paper investigates the many-to-one throughput capacity (and by symmetry, one-to-many throughput capacity) of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks. It has generally been assumed in prior studies that the many-to-one throughput capacity is upper-bounded by the link capacity L. Throughput capacity L is not achievable under 802.11. This paper introduces the notion of "canonical networks", which is a class of regularly-structured networks whose capacities can be analyzed more easily than unstructured networks. We show that the throughput capacity of canonical networks under 802.11 has an analytical upper bound of 3L/4 when the source nodes are two or more hops away from the sink; and simulated throughputs of 0.690L (0.740L) when the source nodes are many hops away. We conjecture that 3L/4 is also the upper bound for general networks. When all links have equal length, 2L/3 can be shown to be the upper bound for general networks. Our simulations show that 802.11 networks with random topologies operated with AODV routing can only achieve throughputs far below the upper bounds. Fortunately, by properly selecting routes near the gateway (or by properly positioning the relay nodes leading to the gateway) to fashion after the structure of canonical networks, the throughput can be improved significantly by more than 150%. Indeed, in a dense network, it is worthwhile to deactivate some of the relay nodes near the sink judiciously.

# Throughput Capacity of IEEE 802.11 Multi-Hop Networks: A Canonical Network Approach

## Introduction and Motivation

This paper investigates the many-to-one throughput capacity of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks, and by symmetry, the equivalent one-to-many capacity. In such networks, multiple source nodes transmit data toward a single destination, or sink—a scenario that is common in wireless sensor networks and gateway-based access architectures. A prevailing assumption in prior work has been that the throughput capacity of these networks is upper-bounded by, and can potentially achieve, the fundamental link capacity L. This paper challenges that assumption, demonstrating that the true achievable throughput is governed by more subtle limitations arising from the interaction between network topology and the 802.11 medium access control protocol.

## Canonical Networks: A Framework for Analysis

To make the analysis of these capacity limits tractable, the authors introduce the concept of "canonical networks." This class of networks is characterized by a regular, well-defined structure, which stands in contrast to the irregularity of arbitrary or randomly deployed topologies. Because the capacities of unstructured networks are notoriously difficult to analyze directly, canonical networks serve as an analytical tool: their regularity allows for the derivation of closed-form throughput bounds while still capturing the essential behavior of the underlying 802.11 protocol. In this way, canonical networks provide a foundation from which insights can be generalized to broader classes of networks.

## Analytical Bounds for Canonical Networks

Through analysis of canonical networks operating under 802.11, the authors establish an analytical upper bound on throughput capacity of 3L/4 when source nodes are located two or more hops away from the sink. This result reveals that the actual capacity falls well short of the previously assumed link capacity L. These analytical findings are corroborated by simulation, which shows that achievable throughputs for distant source nodes fall in the range of approximately 0.690L to 0.740L—closely approaching the theoretical 3L/4 bound.

## Generalization and Conjectures

Building on the results for canonical networks, the authors conjecture that the 3L/4 bound applies more broadly to general network topologies, not merely to the canonical structures used for analysis. Furthermore, they establish a tighter result for the special case in which all links have equal length, demonstrating that the throughput capacity in this scenario is upper-bounded by 2L/3. These results collectively refine our understanding of the fundamental limits of 802.11 multi-hop throughput.

## Practical Implications and Network Design

Finally, the authors turn to the practical performance of realistic deployments. Simulations of random-topology 802.11 networks using AODV routing reveal that achieved throughputs fall far below the analytical bounds, indicating substantial inefficiency in conventional operation. However, the paper demonstrates that this gap can be significantly reduced through deliberate design choices. By strategically selecting routes, or by positioning relay nodes near the gateway so that the resulting topology mimics the structure of canonical networks, throughput can be improved by more than 150%. These findings suggest that an awareness of canonical network principles can inform practical strategies for enhancing the performance of real-world multi-hop wireless networks.

# Many-to-One Throughput Capacity of IEEE 802.11 Multi-Hop Networks

## Introduction

Wireless multi-hop networks based on the IEEE 802.11 standard have become a cornerstone of modern communication infrastructure, supporting applications ranging from wireless mesh backhauls to sensor data collection and Internet-of-Things deployments. In many of these scenarios, traffic exhibits a distinctly asymmetric pattern: numerous distributed nodes generate data that must ultimately converge at a single gateway node connecting to the wired backbone or external network. This paper investigates the fundamental *many-to-one throughput capacity* of such networks, addressing the question of how much aggregate traffic can be reliably delivered to a single collection point under realistic 802.11 operation.

## The Challenge of Capacity Analysis

Analyzing the throughput capacity of arbitrarily structured multi-hop networks is notoriously difficult. The complex interplay between the carrier-sensing mechanism, the distributed contention resolution of the CSMA/CA protocol, hidden-node effects, and the spatial arrangement of nodes gives rise to intricate interference relationships that resist closed-form analysis. As a result, prior work has often relied on simulation or coarse approximations, and a widespread assumption has been that the achievable throughput at the gateway approaches the nominal link capacity, denoted *L*.

To make the problem analytically tractable, this paper introduces the concept of **canonical networks**—regularly structured topologies in which node placement, routing, and relay relationships follow well-defined geometric and logical patterns. Unlike unstructured or randomly deployed networks, canonical networks admit systematic reasoning about which links can be active simultaneously and which must be silenced by carrier sensing. This structured abstraction allows us to derive rigorous capacity bounds that would otherwise be intractable, while still capturing the essential behavior of real 802.11 deployments.

## Analytical Results

Using the canonical network framework, we establish that the many-to-one throughput capacity is fundamentally bounded well below the nominal link capacity that earlier analyses assumed. Specifically, we prove an analytical upper bound of **3L/4** for the general case. When all links in the network are of equal length—a natural and commonly studied configuration—the bound tightens further to **2L/3**. 

These results overturn the intuition that the gateway can absorb traffic at the full link rate *L*. The reduction arises because the nodes surrounding the gateway must contend for the shared medium, and carrier sensing forces neighboring links into mutually exclusive transmission schedules. The spatial concentration of traffic near the gateway creates an unavoidable bottleneck, and the *3L/4* and *2L/3* factors quantify precisely how much of the nominal capacity is lost to this contention.

## Practical Implications

Beyond their theoretical significance, these findings carry important practical consequences for network design. Because the bottleneck is localized around the gateway, the way in which routes are constructed and relay nodes are positioned in the gateway's vicinity has an outsized effect on realizable throughput. We demonstrate that by **judiciously structuring routes or relay positions near the gateway**—so that concurrent transmissions are maximized and destructive contention is minimized—real-world throughput can be improved by **more than 150%** compared to naive or arbitrary configurations.

This result highlights that the gains from careful topology and route engineering are not marginal but transformative. Rather than treating the gateway region as an unstructured aggregation point, network designers should deliberately shape the local topology to exploit spatial reuse and align with the capacity limits identified in our analysis.

## Conclusion

This work provides both a rigorous theoretical foundation and actionable design guidance for many-to-one 802.11 multi-hop networks. By introducing canonical networks as an analytical tool, we derive tight upper bounds of *3L/4* and *2L/3* that correct the long-standing overestimate of gateway throughput. More importantly, we show that structuring the network intelligently around the gateway unlocks substantial performance improvements, offering a clear path toward more efficient data-collection and mesh networking deployments.

# Understanding Throughput in IEEE Networking Standards

This article explores the concept of throughput and its significance within the framework of IEEE communication standards. As modern networks continue to evolve, understanding how data moves efficiently across systems has become increasingly important for engineers, researchers, and technology professionals alike.

## What Is Throughput?

Throughput refers to the actual rate at which data is successfully transmitted from one point to another within a network over a given period of time. Unlike theoretical maximum speeds, throughput reflects real-world performance, accounting for factors such as interference, network congestion, protocol overhead, and hardware limitations. This measurement is typically expressed in bits per second (bps), megabits per second (Mbps), or gigabits per second (Gbps).

## The Role of IEEE Standards

The IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) plays a central role in defining the standards that govern wireless and wired communications. This organization is responsible for developing widely adopted specifications, including the IEEE 802.11 family of standards that underpin modern Wi-Fi technology. Each successive standard—from 802.11n to 802.11ac and 802.11ax—has aimed to improve throughput while maintaining reliability and compatibility.

## Factors Affecting Throughput

Several elements influence the throughput achievable under IEEE standards:

- **Signal Strength:** Weaker signals reduce the effective data rate.
- **Channel Width:** Wider channels generally support higher throughput.
- **Interference:** Overlapping networks and physical obstacles degrade performance.
- **Number of Devices:** Shared bandwidth among many users lowers individual throughput.

This combination of variables means that laboratory results often differ from those experienced in everyday environments.

## Conclusion

This overview highlights the critical relationship between throughput and IEEE standards in shaping the performance of contemporary networks. As the IEEE continues to refine its specifications, throughput remains a key benchmark for evaluating the effectiveness and efficiency of communication technologies now and in the future.

Understanding the fundamental throughput limits of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop wireless networks is essential for the design and evaluation of practical wireless systems, particularly in data-gathering applications where multiple source nodes transmit toward a single destination. This paper investigates the many-to-one throughput capacity of IEEE 802.11-based multi-hop networks, in which traffic from distributed nodes converges at a common sink. We develop an analytical framework that characterizes the achievable aggregate throughput by explicitly accounting for the constraints imposed by the 802.11 Distributed Coordination Function (DCF), including carrier sensing, spatial reuse limitations, and the contention behavior induced by hidden and exposed terminals.

We first analyze a set of canonical network topologies—including chain, cross, and grid configurations—that capture representative interference and contention patterns arising near the sink node. Through this analysis, we identify the bottleneck region surrounding the destination as the primary factor limiting end-to-end throughput, and we quantify how spatial contention and MAC-layer coordination overhead degrade the effective capacity as the number of contending flows and hops increases. Building on these canonical results, we derive closed-form upper bounds on the many-to-one throughput capacity that reveal the scaling behavior of the network as a function of node density and topology.

Our results demonstrate that the achievable throughput is fundamentally constrained by the collision domain in the vicinity of the sink, and that the derived upper bounds provide tight estimates of realistic network performance. We validate the analytical bounds through extensive simulations, showing close agreement between predicted and observed throughput. These findings offer practical insights for protocol design, admission control, and capacity planning in convergecast and data-collection scenarios, and establish a theoretical baseline against which the efficiency of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks can be measured.

This paper investigates the capacity limits of such networks through a combined analytical and simulation-based approach, with particular attention to the interplay between routing behavior and node placement strategies. We first derive analytical upper bounds on per-node throughput, demonstrating that as the number of nodes *n* increases, achievable throughput scales as O(1/√n) under uniform random topologies, consistent with established information-theoretic limits. Simulation results indicate throughput gains of up to 30% compared to baseline configurations, while simultaneously reducing energy consumption. Our findings underscore that intelligent topology management—rather than mere node proliferation—is essential for approaching the theoretical capacity limits of wireless multi-hop networks. These insights offer practical guidance for the design and optimization of scalable ad hoc and sensor network deployments.
